lesson.title: Draining and Filling the Conical Tank
lesson.summary: Water filling a cone-shaped tank rises faster near the narrow bottom and slower near the wide top, and the trick to solving it is using similar triangles to eliminate the radius from the volume formula before differentiating.
lesson.body:
A conical tank, point down, like a funnel, combines two ideas from earlier in this chapter: the similar triangles reasoning from the shadow problem and the volume-formula reasoning from the balloon problem. The tank itself has a fixed shape, a fixed total height H and a fixed radius R at its widest point, the top. At any given moment, the water inside forms a smaller cone of depth h and surface radius r, and because that smaller cone always has the same proportions as the full tank, r and h are related by similar triangles: r / h = R / H, so r = (R/H) h.

This substitution matters because the volume of a cone is V = (1/3) pi r^2 h, which involves two changing quantities, r and h, but only one equation for volume, dV/dt. With two unknowns and one equation, differentiating directly would leave an extra unknown rate, dr/dt, sitting in the result. Substituting r = (R/H) h first eliminates r entirely, rewriting the volume purely in terms of h: V = (1/3) pi ((R/H) h)^2 h = (1/3) pi (R/H)^2 h^3, a single-variable relationship that can be differentiated cleanly, exactly the same move as recognizing similar triangles gave a hidden constraint equation back in implicit-in-context.

Here is the fully worked example. A conical tank, point down, has a total height of 10 meters and a top radius of 5 meters. Water flows in at a rate of 10 cubic meters per minute. Find the rate at which the water depth is rising at the moment the depth is 4 meters. First find the ratio R/H = 5/10 = 1/2, so r = h/2 at every instant. Substitute into the volume formula: V = (1/3) pi (h/2)^2 h = (1/3) pi (h^2/4) h = pi h^3 / 12. Differentiate with respect to t: dV/dt = (pi/12)(3h^2)(dh/dt) = (pi h^2 / 4)(dh/dt). Substitute dV/dt = 10 and h = 4: 10 = (pi (16) / 4)(dh/dt) = 4 pi (dh/dt). Solving: dh/dt = 10 / (4 pi) = 5 / (2 pi) meters per minute, approximately 0.796 meters per minute.

The physical picture behind the algebra is worth stating plainly: near the bottom of the cone, where h is small, the tank is very narrow, so a fixed inflow rate makes the water level shoot up quickly. Near the top, where h is large, the cone has widened out considerably, so the same inflow rate raises the level far more slowly. This is the same underlying idea as the balloon problem, a fixed rate of volume change spread across a changing cross section, except here the relevant cross section is the horizontal circle of radius r = h/2 rather than the full surface area of a sphere.
